Miriam
MIR-ee-uhm
proper noun
Hebrew Mirām, of uncertain sense, perhaps “bitter” or “beloved”; the same name carried into Greek as Mariam and so into the New Testament as Mary.

See also: Miriam

Biblical Definition

Miriam was the sister of Moses and Aaron, the daughter of Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi. As a girl she watched over the ark of bulrushes among the reeds of the Nile and wisely offered to fetch a Hebrew nurse for the infant Moses, so that his own mother was paid to raise him. After the crossing of the Red Sea she is called a prophetess, and she took a timbrel in her hand and led the women of Israel in the song of triumph, answering Moses’ song with the refrain, “Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously.” Yet she is also a warning. When she and Aaron spoke against Moses over the matter of his wife, jealous of his unique mediation, the anger of the LORD was kindled, and Miriam was struck with leprosy white as snow. Moses cried for her healing, and after seven days shut out of the camp she was received again. She died at Kadesh and was buried there. The dictionary remembers her both as a woman honored in the deliverance and song of Israel and as a solemn example that the LORD will vindicate His appointed servants against the murmuring even of their own kin.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sister of Moses and Aaron, a prophetess who led Israel’s women in song after the Red Sea, and who was later struck with leprosy for speaking against Moses.

expand to see more

MIRIAM, n. The elder sister of Moses and Aaron, of the tribe of Levi.

As a child she watched the ark of bulrushes and procured her own mother as nurse for the infant Moses.

Called a prophetess; she led the women of Israel with timbrels in the song of triumph at the Red Sea.

Smitten with leprosy for seven days when she and Aaron murmured against the prophet Moses.

Died and was buried at Kadesh; remembered among the deliverers God set over Israel in the exodus.

Key Scripture

Exo 15:20 — "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances."

Exo 15:21 — "And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea."

Num 12:1 — "And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman."

Mic 6:4 — "For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam."

Modern Corruption

Miriam is conscripted as a banner for overturning the order God set in Israel, against the plain lesson of her chastening.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption seizes upon Miriam’s title “prophetess” to argue that Scripture sanctions women in the ruling and teaching offices over men, and reads her complaint against Moses as a righteous bid for equal authority. The text says the opposite. When Miriam and Aaron challenged the singular mediation God had given Moses—“Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses?”—the LORD came down, vindicated His servant, and struck Miriam with leprosy. The chapter is a divine rebuke of the very ambition the corruption celebrates.

The honest reading honors Miriam without unmaking the order of Scripture. God did use her, gift her, and name her among Israel’s deliverers through Micah; women prophesied in both Testaments. But the office of teaching elder and the headship of the home and church belong, by God’s appointment, to qualified men. Miriam’s leprosy is the standing answer to every attempt to make her the patroness of egalitarian revolt; the dictionary lets the warning stand beside the honor.

Hebrew Roots

Her name, the Hebrew form of Mary, is of debated sense and was borne by many daughters of Israel down to the mother of our Lord.

expand to see more

Hebrew Mirām — the proper name, variously explained as “bitter,” “beloved,” or “rebellion.”

Some derive it from mārāh, to be bitter, recalling the bitterness of bondage in Egypt.

Others connect it with a root for “beloved” or “wished-for child.”

The Greek Mariam carries the name into the New Testament as Mary.

Thus the prophetess of the exodus and the virgin mother of Christ share one ancient Hebrew name.

Usage

"Miriam’s song at the sea is a model of corporate praise for God’s mighty acts of deliverance."

"Numbers twelve is preached to warn against murmuring jealousy of God’s appointed leaders."

"Her name is noted as the Hebrew original of Mary, the most common woman’s name in first-century Judea."
